analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for generic drug makers to get brand-name samples needed to develop cheaper copies.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in March 2023 with one Democrat and one Republican behind it, never received a Senate committee vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it harder for brand-name drug companies to stall generic competition. Under current law, brand companies must sell samples of their drugs to generic makers who need them to develop and test lower-cost copies, and this bill would close common evasions: it would bar companies from using contract terms to refuse, let generic makers send requests by tracked overnight delivery, require them to publish who handles requests, and cut the Food and Drug Administration's wait time for approving sample requests for safety-restricted drugs from 120 days to 60 when no human trials are involved. It was referred to the Senate health committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who would get cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars sooner, because the bill removes tools brand companies can use to slow the arrival of lower-cost competition: refusing to sell samples, imposing restrictive contract terms, ignoring or slow-walking written requests, and lengthy FDA waits for safety-restricted (REMS) drugs. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers, which must buy these samples to develop products, also gain directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients waiting for cheaper generic drugs

how_it_helps.text: Forces brand-name companies to sell samples on commercially reasonable, market-based terms and adds restrictive 'contractual terms' imposed by the license holder to the conditions that count as an unlawful refusal to provide samples.

Lets generic developers send purchase requests through tracked overnight or 2-day delivery services ('designated delivery services'), and allows repeated requests at each stage of development, so brand companies cannot quietly ignore requests or let them sit unopened in a mailroom.

Cuts the FDA's deadline for authorizing access to samples of safety-restricted (REMS with ETASU) drugs from 120 days to 60 days when testing does not involve human clinical trials, speeding development of generics for drugs that are hard to study.

Requires each brand company to publicly post its policy for handling sample requests, with contact information, procedures, and the name of the corporate officer responsible — making refusals and delays visible and attributable.

Extends the same protections to biosimilar developers, including treating a brand product's packaging, devices, and accessories as part of what must be provided, which matters for copycat versions of biologic drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which lose some of the practical ways to delay generic and biosimilar competition — refusing sample sales via contract terms, ignoring written requests, and long FDA waits for safety-restricted drugs. Any resulting revenue loss shows up as shorter periods of monopoly pricing before cheaper copies reach the market.

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrow: it only helps generic development where sample access is the bottleneck, and does nothing about the biggest price drivers — patent thickets, pay-for-delay settlements, or pharmacy middlemen — so its effect on drug prices would be modest and incremental.

It compresses FDA review of sample requests for safety-restricted (REMS with ETASU) drugs from 120 days to 60 in non-human-trial cases, giving the agency less time to confirm that a generic developer's handling of a risky drug meets the safety conditions the brand version is subject to.

It imposes new compliance duties on brand companies — public sample-access policies, named responsible officers, and acceptance of courier deliveries at any development stage — an administrative cost, though a small one relative to what the companies currently charge for their drugs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A well-targeted, low-risk fix. The costs are an administrative burden on brand manufacturers and a slightly faster clock at the FDA for safety-restricted drugs; the benefit is that generics and biosimilars reach patients sooner and cheaper. The main honest criticism is scale: it patches one workaround in the generic-approval process rather than addressing the largest causes of high drug prices, so patients should not expect dramatic savings from it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2023, sent to the Senate health committee, and the committee never took it up, so it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Maggie Hassan introduced the bill on March 30, 2023, joined by Republican Senator Mike Braun, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — the action history ends with the referral, and the bill expired with the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because the existing tools this bill would have restricted — refusing or slow-walking sample requests and lengthy waits for safety-restricted drugs — remain available, and cheaper generic competition keeps arriving later than it otherwise might.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill on March 30, 2023.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, its only Republican support.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 30, 2023 and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill sat for 21 months until the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.what_they_did: Led the committee that took no action on the bill after referral; nothing in the record shows the bill was prioritized for a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only sponsor was a Democrat and its only cosponsor a Republican, but because no committee or floor vote ever occurred, the chamber's partisan breakdown on it is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would strip away several practical ways to delay generic competition — refusing to sell samples through contract terms, ignoring or slow-walking written requests, and lengthy FDA waits for safety-restricted drugs — shortening the period of monopoly pricing. Its interest in preserving those delays runs directly against patients paying brand prices.

These companies must buy brand-name samples to develop and test copies, and the bill makes those samples easier to get and requests harder to ignore. Faster generic development is exactly how their product pipeline advances, which is also when patients see savings.

The bill defines a class of tracked overnight and 2-day delivery services as the official channel for sample requests, creating a small new business use for couriers like these. A minor effect alongside the main provisions.
